scenes.tts: How can a cell halve its chromosome sets without losing any chromosome type? Watch this cell carry a large pair and a small pair. Green chromosomes came from one parent. Orange chromosomes came from the other. Every pair carries the same kinds of genes.
scenes.visual: Hook first, no separate title card. A large cell fills 70% of frame height. Inside, one long green rod faces one long orange rod; one short green rod faces one short orange rod. Brackets join each size-matched pair. Slowly orbit the four rods. Title appears small at top after the question. Color map begins: green = chromosome inherited from one parent; orange = chromosome inherited from the other; blue = cell boundary; yellow = current action.
scenes.narration: How can a cell halve its chromosome sets without losing any chromosome type? Watch this cell carry a large pair and a small pair. Green chromosomes came from one parent. Orange chromosomes came from the other. Every pair carries the same kinds of genes.

scenes.tts: The partners in each pair are homologous chromosomes. They carry genes in matching positions, but their alleles may differ. An allele is a version of a gene. Matching does not mean identical; homologs can carry different instructions for a trait. The starting cell is diploid because it has both members of every pair.
scenes.visual: Zoom to the long pair. Matching gene-position bands slide onto both rods, aligned horizontally. At one band, green gains allele label A and orange gains allele label a. Pull back to both pairs. A brace groups the green-and-orange set as DIPLOID. Keep rods drifting gently.
scenes.narration: The partners in each pair are homologous chromosomes. They carry genes in matching positions, but their alleles may differ. An allele is a version of a gene. Matching does not mean identical; homologs can carry different instructions for a trait. The starting cell is diploid because it has both members of every pair.

scenes.tts: Before meiosis, each chromosome copies its D N A. Each rod becomes joined sister chromatids. The D N A amount doubled, but the chromosome count did not. An ex shape shows a copied chromosome, not a homologous pair. Count joined sister chromatids as one chromosome until their connection separates.
scenes.caption: Before meiosis, each chromosome copies its DNA. Each rod becomes joined sister chromatids. The DNA amount doubled, but the chromosome count did not. An X shape shows a copied chromosome, not a homologous pair. Count joined sister chromatids as one chromosome until their connection separates.
scenes.visual: Each rod smoothly duplicates and hinges into an X shape. A yellow copy sweep passes left to right. A tracker reads CHROMOSOMES: unchanged while a second line reads DNA: doubled. Highlight one centromere joining two sister chromatids. Do not draw DNA structure.
scenes.narration: Before meiosis, each chromosome copies its DNA. Each rod becomes joined sister chromatids. The DNA amount doubled, but the chromosome count did not. An X shape shows a copied chromosome, not a homologous pair. Count joined sister chromatids as one chromosome until their connection separates.

scenes.tts: Now the homologous chromosomes meet as pairs. In the first division, each homolog moves away from its partner. The green long chromosome can travel with the orange short chromosome. The other homologs travel to the opposite side.
scenes.visual: The two homologous X pairs align at the cell center. Yellow spindle-like arrows point toward opposite sides without molecular detail. Long green and short orange X shapes glide left; long orange and short green glide right. The cell pinches into two large daughter cells.
scenes.narration: Now the homologous chromosomes meet as pairs. In the first division, each homolog moves away from its partner. The green long chromosome can travel with the orange short chromosome. The other homologs travel to the opposite side.

scenes.tts: Each new cell now has a member of every homologous pair, still made of joined sisters. What must separate in the next division? Follow the yellow connection in each ex shape.
scenes.caption: Each new cell now has a member of every homologous pair, still made of joined sisters. What must separate in the next division? Follow the yellow connection in each X shape.
scenes.visual: Hold the two daughter cells side by side. Each contains one long X and one short X. The centromere connection on every X pulses yellow. Show the question: WHAT SEPARATES NEXT? Gentle cell-boundary motion continues.
scenes.narration: Each new cell now has a member of every homologous pair, still made of joined sisters. What must separate in the next division? Follow the yellow connection in each X shape.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep WHAT SEPARATES NEXT? on screen. The four yellow centromere connections pulse slowly; everything else remains stable.

scenes.tts: The sister chromatids separate next. No DNA copying happens between the divisions. Each cell divides again as the joined copies pull apart. The finished cells hold a single chromosome from every original pair.
scenes.visual: In both cells, each X splits at its yellow connection into two rods. Rods move to opposite halves while both cells pinch simultaneously. Finish with four cells in a square, each containing one long rod and one short rod.
scenes.narration: The sister chromatids separate next. No DNA copying happens between the divisions. Each cell divides again as the joined copies pull apart. The finished cells hold a single chromosome from every original pair.

scenes.tts: These cells are haploid because each has a single chromosome set. In the simple animal model, the completed divisions usually produce a group of haploid cells. Human egg formation is uneven, and plants make spores instead of gametes. Those refinements do not change the separation rule.
scenes.visual: Label the four-cell result HAPLOID. Then transform the four equal cells into a small schematic inset: one large egg with two or three tiny polar bodies, labelled SCHEMATIC. Beside it, a plant spore icon appears, also labelled SCHEMATIC. Return to the four-cell model.
scenes.narration: These cells are haploid because each has a single chromosome set. In the simple animal model, the completed divisions usually produce a group of haploid cells. Human egg formation is uneven, and plants make spores instead of gametes. Those refinements do not change the separation rule.

scenes.tts: Meiosis separates pairs, then copies. The first division separates homologous pairs and halves the chromosome sets. The second separates the sister chromatids of each copied chromosome. This is not mitosis repeated, because mitosis never separates homologous pairs.
scenes.visual: Build a two-step pathway from the carried model: PAIRED HOMOLOGS transform into SEPARATED PAIRS, then JOINED SISTERS transform into SEPARATED COPIES. The first arrow glows yellow, then the second. Briefly show MITOSIS beside it with homologs never pairing, then fade that comparison.
scenes.narration: Meiosis separates pairs, then copies. The first division separates homologous pairs and halves the chromosome sets. The second separates the sister chromatids of each copied chromosome. This is not mitosis repeated, because mitosis never separates homologous pairs.

scenes.tts: When egg and sperm later join, their haploid sets restore a diploid cell. Halving keeps chromosome number from doubling each generation. The products can carry different chromosome mixes. The next film asks why those products carry different allele mixes.
scenes.visual: Two haploid model cells glide together and merge into one diploid cell, restoring green-orange homologous pairs. A small generation loop stays level instead of rising. Then fan the earlier products behind it as two complementary green-orange combinations, with each combination repeated.
scenes.narration: When egg and sperm later join, their haploid sets restore a diploid cell. Halving keeps chromosome number from doubling each generation. The products can carry different chromosome mixes. The next film asks why those products carry different allele mixes.

scenes.visual: End card shows one centered line only: 'Meiosis separates pairs, then copies.' No subtitle, logo, or smaller line.
